newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: German "superspy" taken to Bogota safe house.
newsitem.headline: German "superspy" taken to Bogota safe house.

text.p: German diplomatic sources on Sunday welcomed the release of German "superspy" Werner Mauss and his wife and said the couple would stay in a Bogota safe house until kidnap-related charges against them were resolved.
"The German government is pleased that they have been freed and recognise it as a gesture of good will on the part of the Colombian authorities," a spokesman at the German Embassy in Bogota said.
"The Mausses are not in any danger, but for reasons of security, we are not going to say where they are," he added.

Mauss and his wife, Michaela, flew to Bogota from the northwest city of Medellin on Sunday morning aboard a charter flight with their lawyer, Abraham Casallas, and Medellin-based honorary consul Helmut Luecker.

The group left the airport by an emergency exit without making any comments to the media. The four did not go to either the main embassy building or the German ambassador's residence, as it had been widely rumoured they might.

The Mausses were arrested just outside Medellin in November 1996 while trying to bundle German kidnap victim Brigitte Schoene -- wife of a former BASF Chemicals executive -- aboard a plane leaving the country.
Schoene was kidnapped several months earlier by suspected members of the National Liberation Army (ELN), Colombia's second-largest guerrilla group.

The Mausses were released from Itagui top-security prison early on Saturday after a successful habeas corpus appeal and spent much of the day by the pool of one of Medellin's top hotels, local media reported.

They still face trial on charges of using false documents and personally benefiting from an abduction -- a reference to receiving a fee for the release of a kidnap victim. Charges of kidnap, extortion and conspiracy to kidnap have been dropped.

Mauss was briefly linked to Germany's secret services and has close ties to Bernd Schmidbauer, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's head of intelligence services. The connections led the German and Colombian media to dub him a James Bond-style superspy.
